notes:
I ran out of searches and page reads before I could cover everything. Below I've only written up what the pages I read actually say. I read three pages in full, but each one cut off partway through the chapter: Enduring Word (David Guzik) stops around v. 15, Bible.org's commentary at v. 10, and the Pulpit Commentary at v. 8. For the later verses I'm working from short search-result excerpts, and some of the Enduring Word material comes from its Spanish edition, which I've put into English.

**Not found at all:** NET Bible notes; Lutheran, Pentecostal, Methodist and Reformed readings stated by their own teachers; Orthodox readings (oca.org); and anything on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching. Verse 18 has no notes.

---

**v. 1**
- Jesus' tomb stayed sealed and guarded by Roman soldiers until it was found open early on the first day of the week. Other Gospels say at least three other women came with Mary, but John names her because she was the one who ran to tell the disciples. Jesus had cast seven demons out of her, and that past didn't stop her becoming the first witness of the resurrection. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-20/
- "Still dark" seems to clash with Mark 16:2, which says the sun had risen. Bible.org gives harmless explanations: the path may still have been dark, John may mean when she left home, or the women may have come in separate groups. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-20
- All the Gospels agree on the day, which became "the Lord's day." Mary probably went ahead of the other women. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/john/20.htm

**v. 2**
- Mary assumed the body had been stolen. She wasn't hoping for a resurrection and didn't imagine one. The "we" fits Mark's account that she wasn't alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-20/
- She may have gone to Peter and John simply because she knew where they were. This verse is the first to identify the "other disciple" as the one Jesus loved. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-20
- The word for "loved" here is the word for personal affection. On this reading, John isn't putting himself above Peter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/john/20.htm

**vv. 3–4**
- John modestly doesn't name himself, yet he still notes that he outran Peter. Tradition makes Peter the older man. Both clearly ran hard because they had to see for themselves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-20/
- The verse is the main reason John is pictured as young, but it says nothing about his age. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-20
- Pulpit takes the opposite view: John, the younger man, naturally outran Peter, and the detail is lifelike. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/john/20.htm

**v. 5**
- "Looked" translates the Greek word *blepei*, meaning to see clearly. Tenney (quoted by Guzik) suggests John stayed outside out of respect for the dead or fear of becoming ritually unclean. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-20/
- Tomb entrances were usually under 3 feet high, so you had to bend down. John gives no reason why he didn't go in. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-20
- Pulpit suggests awe and dawning hope. It cites Wettstein (an 18th-century scholar) on fear of becoming unclean. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/john/20.htm

**vv. 6–7**
- Peter went straight in, as was typical of him. His "saw" (*theorei*) means he studied the scene. The cloths lay in order, as if the body had passed through them, which a grave robber wouldn't do. Separate head and body cloths raise a question about the Shroud of Turin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-20/
- Bible.org doubts the "body passed through the cloths" idea. It reads v. 7 as saying the head cloth lay in a different place. Either way, the neat cloths showed thieves hadn't taken the body. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-20
- Pulpit agrees: the scene showed care, not haste. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/john/20.htm

**v. 8**
- John's "saw" (*eiden*) means he grasped what it meant. Unusually, he believed before meeting the risen Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-20/
- Bible.org rejects the idea that John merely believed Mary's report. It says he believed in the resurrection because of the orderly grave clothes. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-20
- **Older division:** Pulpit says Augustine, Erasmus and Luther held that John believed Mary's report. Others, following Chrysostom, held that he believed Jesus had risen, and Pulpit sides with them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/john/20.htm

**v. 9**
- They believed the fact but didn't yet understand its meaning from Scripture. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-20/
- John doesn't name the Scriptures. Possibilities include Isaiah 53:10–12, Psalm 16:10, Jonah 1:17 and Hosea 6:2. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-20
- Pink sees a contrast between faith resting on God's Word and mere outward evidence. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/awp/john-20.html

**v. 10**
- John doesn't say what the two were thinking. Luke 24:12 says Peter went home wondering. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-20

**vv. 11–13**
- Mary wept because she didn't yet believe. She may not have realised these were angels. Adam Clarke compares their places, at head and feet, to the cherubim on the mercy seat. She only wanted to find the body to finish the burial. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-20/

**vv. 14–15**
- Leon Morris (quoted by Guzik) says something about the risen Jesus meant he wasn't always recognised. Jesus held back from revealing himself in order to break through her unbelief, not to trick her. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-20/
- Some think her tears blinded her; others that Jesus looked different. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/juan-20/
- Jesus' first words after rising were meant to comfort human grief. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/john/20.htm

**v. 16**
- Through her tears Mary saw only a man, until one word filled her with sudden joy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/john/20.htm
- Mary, once troubled by demons, became the first witness. No one inventing the story would pick a woman, since women's testimony wasn't legally accepted then. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-20/

**v. 17**
- The sense is not that her touch would defile him. Mary had grabbed hold of Jesus and didn't want to let go. The verse also shows his body was real, not a ghost's. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/juan-20/
- Pulpit says the verb describes a continuing state rather than a single act. The key word is "not yet": after he ascends, there will be lasting spiritual fellowship with him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/john/20.htm

**v. 19**
- Locked doors didn't hold the risen Jesus back, which hints at what our resurrection bodies will be like. He sought out his people. Spurgeon notes that Jesus came to show them nothing but himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-20/
- "Peace" was the ordinary greeting, but here it recalled John 14:27 and calmed their fear. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/john/20.htm
- His first word on the new day was peace, a pledge of the future. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/awp/john-20.html

**v. 20**
- Verse 25 shows these were the nail marks and the spear wound. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-20
- By showing them, Jesus assured them he really was Jesus of Nazareth, risen. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/juan-20/

**v. 21**
- Pulpit, following Westcott, says the two Greek verbs for "send" carry slightly different shades of meaning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/john/20.htm
- The commission parallels John 17:18 and is probably for all followers, like Matthew 28. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-20
- Guzik also says Jesus sends every believer. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/juan-20/
- Matthew Henry sees Christ's divinity here: his commissions carry the Father's authority. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_020.cfm

**v. 22**
- Guzik sees a deliberate link to God breathing life into man at creation. Tenney (quoted) says the Spirit was given to empower the church's mission, not as an ornament. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/juan-20/
- Bible.org says the action symbolises the new creation Jesus began. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-20
- I found nothing comparing this verse with Pentecost (Acts 2) from any tradition.

**v. 23 (the main dividing verse)**
- **Evangelical:** Morris (quoted by Guzik) says the Spirit-filled church has authority to declare which sins are forgiven or retained, like rabbis calling sins "bound" or "loosed." https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/juan-20/
- The Expositor's Bible Commentary says the verse has caused endless controversy. Its view: the apostles were agents who announced the terms for entering Christ's kingdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/john/20.htm
- Bible.org translates it "have been forgiven" and links it to Matthew 16:19 and 18:18. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-20
- **Catholic:** Jesus gave the apostles and their successors the ministry of forgiving sins, including power to withhold forgiveness from someone who hasn't truly repented. https://www.catholic.com/bible-navigator/confession/john2021-23
- Catholic writers also argue that confessing sins aloud is implied, since the apostles would have to hear the sins first. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/is-confession-in-scripture
- **Protestant replies, as catholic.com reports them:** the main one is that the verse means preaching forgiveness, with God forgiving or not depending on how hearers respond. https://www.catholic.com/audio/scw/is-confession-biblical-debunking-protestant-comebacks-to-john-2023
- A second reply relies on Greek grammar: the verbs mean God has already forgiven, and the apostles only declare it. Catholic writers answer from 1 John 2:5 and Luke 7:47. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/a-biblical-case-for-confession
- Catholic.com quotes Got Questions' objections: the verse never mentions confession and never mentions successors. It answers with a quote from Chrysostom and one from the Baptist scholar George Beasley-Murray. https://www.catholic.com/audio/cot/3-reasons-to-confess-your-sins-to-a-priest
- (I didn't read the Protestant objectors' own pages.)

**vv. 24–25**
- The disciples welcomed Thomas in and invited him to "come and see." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_020.cfm
- Guzik calls Thomas's demand for proof stubborn refusal, not mere doubt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-20/

**v. 26**
- F. F. Bruce (quoted by Guzik) suggests that memory of this visit may lie behind the early church meeting on Sunday evenings and praying *Marana tha*, "Our Lord, come!" https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/juan-20/

**v. 27**
- Jesus met Thomas with mercy, repeating Thomas's own conditions back to him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-20/
- Jesus was gracious but didn't praise his unbelief. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/juan-20/
- Matthew Henry reads it as "do not become an unbeliever." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_020.cfm

**v. 28**
- No deeper statement of who Jesus is could be made. It echoes John 1:1 and 1:14 together. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-20

**v. 29**
- Jesus said "because you have seen," not "seen and touched," which suggests Thomas may never have touched the wounds. Those who accept reliable eyewitness testimony are blessed. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/juan-20/
- Jesus turns to the wider audience: everyone who will believe through the disciples' word. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-20

**vv. 30–31**
- Faith in Jesus as Messiah and God brings the promise of life. "In his name" means through the person himself, not just by saying his name. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/juan-20/
- Matthew Henry says this life includes both spiritual life now and eternal life. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_020.cfm
- Bible.org lists studies on whether v. 31 means "come to believe" or "keep believing," but I didn't reach its notes on the question. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-20
